Multiplayer:

Multiplayer has been CoD's biggest emphasis in recent games, and Black Ops 3 is no different. Multiplayer in BO3 is a series of small refinements without going too far into uncharted territory. Maps are pretty well laid out, following the same "three lane" layout from previous Black Ops games. BO3 takes a small page out of Modern Warfare's book, and avoids creating maps that "funnel" you towards the enemy in straight lines, which has been my minor complaint for Black Ops 1 and 2.
Jetpacks are back again, in the form of a "momentum based movement" system. In Advanced Warfare, the jetpack was more of an evasion tool; you could use the jetpack to jump quickly into the air and rain bullets down on your enemy while dodging fire. The jetpack in BO3 is more of a movement aide, allowing you to jump and wallrun in more gradual arcs, abandoning the abrupt jumps and dodges of Advanced Warfare.
Multiplayer is pretty well balanced, and they didn't mess with it much aside from the momentum system. You have your choice of primary (SMG, Assault Rifle, Shotgun, LMG, Sniper Rifle) and secondary (Pistols, Launchers). All of your skills and weapon attachments cost some of your allotted equipment points, so you have a bit of freedom to forgo certain gear in order to bring more of something else.

Zombies:

Zombies is back in pretty much the same form it has existed in previous Black Ops games. There's only one map for the moment, but it's a big one, allowing you and your buddies to spread out and explore, if you're feeling adventurous. There's no custom classes here, just guns that you find on the walls in the level. You can customize "Gobblegum", which dispenses from machines in-game and provides you with temporary skill boosts to keep alive.

Campaign:

Here's where the real changes are. Call of Duty hasn't had co-op campaign since World at War, and where that was more of an afterthought, BO3 embraces co-op gameplay from the ground up. The levels are a little more open than the "corridor shooter" style of previous games, which allows you and your buddies to spread out a bit and cover ground differently. Custom classes are also available in the campaign, allowing you to specialize your skills and weaponry however you like. The story allows you to select missions in any order, but there's no reason not to play the whole plot in order either. The setting of the game is the same "future soldier" theme from Black Ops 2 and Advanced Warfare, but this time Treyarch has done a great job of making the technology theme feel integrated into the story, and not just layered on as a gimmick. The futuristic technology doesn't feel out of place, and you quickly accept its role in the story. There's a lot of plot to take in right off the bat, but if you like an action-focused plot with a few twists thrown in, grab a buddy or two and give campaign a try. You'll notice more on the second playthrough than the first, for sure.

Nightmare Mode (New Game+):

Nightmare mode is the New Game+ mode that unlocks after you beat the campaign. It tells the story of an alternate timeline where zombies have replaced the usual enemies in each campaign mission. You have no custom classes in this game mode, relying on weapon drops and mystery boxes to supply your weapons randomly. The narration was my favorite part, because the in-game custscenes remain in place; Nightmare Mode simply mutes the speaker and talks over the soundtrack with a zombie-focused narration. Sometimes the narrator will have to work hard to explain away a plot point from the normal story, or explain why one of your "allied zombie hunters" just stabbed his comrade in the shoulder during a cut-scene. It's a little goofy, but something you can have fun with.

Overall Impressions:

Black Ops 3 is a complete package, even if you don't care for one of the game modes. Multiplayer is stronger than ever without doing too much to mess up the formula, co-op gameplay and custom classes breathe new life into campaign, and Nightmare Mode is a welcome addition to the undead gameplay of the usual zombies mode.

So one of my players is arguing that Moonbeam does damage when cast and then again at the start of the turn of the creature in it. He believes that since the spell requires concentration and an action to move, that justifies the damage. Also, he feels as if when the spell says "When a creature enters the spell's area for the first time on a turn...", it's implying when the beam is created, the creature is considered to be "entering" it since it is engulfed inside the beam. I completely disagree. If something is entering, then it is moving, not the beam. It's similar to Attacks of Opportunity (AO). AO's state that when a creature leaves your reach, you get to make an AO. One could technically say that as I walk away and provoke an AO, the other creature is leaving my reach also, so I should get to make an AO. That's not how AO's work and that's not how that spell works. It's similar concepts. The "...enters the spell's area.." is for if it voluntarily enters or is forced to enter via shove, spell, etc.

His interpretation also falls to pieces due to how different it can be due to initiative. If he's directly before the creature, that means he's doing guaranteed 4d10/2 according to his interpretation. That's a wicked amount of damage for a level 2 spell, that happens to cover a 10x10 zone, is of a damage type that is rarely resisted, and especially since it's guaranteed.

I've tried googling it, but people generally only have an issue with others moving it around and sweeping an area so they can try to do 2d10 on each enemy possible. We've actually just not worried about it and said it disappears from one area and appears at its final destination. If that's wrong, then let me know. Being able to move it over creatures effectively makes it stronger than a fighter since it does 2d10/2 to every creature that succeeds the save. He could just sweep the enter enemy army and just about one shot everything on the map. A fighter could only do 2d10 to a single creature if it crit and if he missed, then there would be no damage. This also raises the question of if the beam is moved on top of an enemy in general, does it do damage? I would say "no" because it would contradict my reasoning for it not doing damage when cast. The beam is moving. Not the creature. That would also prevent sweeping with the beam. That brings up the point of "What is really the difference between the beam moving over an enemy and an enemy entering it? The enemy is in the beam regardless." I'm sure you can see how confusing and frustrating this is. The wording is just vague enough.

As you can probably tell, I have become increasingly frustrated over this debate. Despite which you agree with, please provide citations when possible so that I can go back to him and say "This is what I'm ruling and this is why." I don't care who's right. I just want to make sure we're doing the right thing.

  • Spell: first time on a turn
